content.p: On the morning of Tuesday 5 August 1873, a Pawnee hunting party of roughly 350 men, women and children was moving slowly up a canyon in the Republican River country of southwestern Nebraska, heading for the divide that separates that valley from the Frenchman. They had spent a month on the buffalo range and were on their way home. That same day, a Sioux force of more than a thousand warriors overran them. The army's own count of the dead came to 63; the Pawnee agent later counted 69.

Writers on the subject usually rank it as the final big clash of one tribe against another anywhere in the United States. The Nebraska historian Paul Riley, writing for the state historical society in 1973, described it as a surprise attack. By the army's count, most of the dead were women and children.
content.h2: A people squeezed on every side
content.p: The Pawnee had once been the most powerful nation in Nebraska. By the 1870s disease and warfare had cut their numbers and their influence. Since the Civil War they had sided with the whites, and some of their men had served in the army as scouts under Major Frank North. That service did nothing to lessen the old hatred between them and the Sioux and Cheyenne, whom the scouts had helped to hunt.

The Nebraska Studies history of the two peoples puts the Pawnee at 10,000 to 12,000 in Nebraska by 1800, living in four bands (Chaui, Kitkehahki, Pirahauerat and Skidi). Smallpox and other diseases then cut their numbers by half, and by the 1830s the better-armed, nomadic Lakota were raiding their Loup River villages. The Oklahoma Historical Society's encyclopedia adds that the Pawnee supplied scouts to the army in the Plains wars, because of the pressure from the Sioux, including ninety-five men in the 1865-66 Powder River Expedition.

A treaty signed with Washington in 1857 had placed the Pawnee on a reservation in present Nance County, east-central Nebraska. The government had promised to protect them from their enemies. In practice, the Loup River and its forks served as a natural road between the reservation and the Brule and Oglala Sioux of the north, and raiding parties used it. Pawnee women were killed in their cornfields and horses were stolen. White settlers added their own pressure, stripping the reservation's timber and pasturing livestock on its remote corners.

The Pawnee were administered by a succession of Quaker agents under President Ulysses S. Grant's Indian policy. The agents urged peace and disapproved of the hunt, which took people out of their control. Riley notes that in the main the Pawnee did keep the peace, though bands of young men slipped away on horse-stealing raids of their own. In 1871 the agent Jacob Troth relayed a government proposal for a peace treaty with Spotted Tail's Brule. Sky Chief, a chief of the Republican, or Kitkehahki, band, doubted that Spotted Tail was telling the truth, and said so at a council. The treaty never went beyond talk.

The Pawnee still depended on two hunts a year for their meat: a summer hunt beginning around the first of July once the crops were planted, and a winter hunt from early November. As white settlement moved up the Republican valley, and as professional hide hunters slaughtered the herds by the thousand, the Pawnee had to travel farther west each year. That brought them into the country where Oglala and Brule bands also hunted.

The summer hunt of 1872 went well. The Pawnee, joined by a party of Ponca, travelled with the frontiersman John "Texas Jack" Omohundro as trail agent and checked in with the army at Camp Red Willow. In a letter to the Omaha Herald, the sawmill owner W. M. Hinman wrote that 2,700 Pawnee and Ponca had stopped at the settlement for a few days, killing 200 or 300 buffalo and driving off some cattle. A man from Franklin County, J. F. Zediker, wrote to the press in a very different spirit, complaining of reservation Indians passing through the valley several times a year to beg, plunder and kill game. Riley sets Hinman's tolerance against the opinion he says most frontier letter-writers held.

The winter hunt, which began in mid-November 1872, was a disaster. No trail agent had been appointed, since Omohundro had left to join Buffalo Bill Cody on the stage in the East. In early January, while the Pawnee were hunting on foot, Sioux raiders stole more than a hundred of their horses. One of four Pawnee youths who chased the thieves was killed, apparently drawn into a trap. The Pawnee had to cache their meat and equipment and walk home. Riley judges the loss a blow to both the Pawnee economy and their pride. A confusing story ran alongside it: three Oglala, among them a man named Whistler, had been murdered by white hunters that winter, and the press at the time muddled that killing with the raid on the Pawnee. Riley says there was much speculation about who the killers were, and that contemporaries and the press thought the likeliest were the hunters Mortimer Kress and John Ralston.

By summer 1873 the Pawnee were so poor that their new Quaker agent, William Burgess, found their poverty a shock. When the chiefs asked to go out again, they requested John Williamson as trail agent. Williamson, 23, born in Wisconsin and by then working as a farmer at the Genoa agency, said later that he had not applied. Burgess's letter of instruction, dated 2 July, told him not to interfere with the Pawnee's usual hunting methods but authorised him to advise them and take every precaution against incursions by their enemies. The McCook Gazette's centennial article, reprinted on the NEGenWeb site, thought the choice unfortunate: Williamson was liked by the Pawnee but new to the frontier, and he was probably picked because they knew he would not push his opinions.

The party left the reservation on 3 July, according to Riley. Accounts of its makeup differ. The McCook Gazette's centennial article says Sky Chief led, aided by Sun Chief and Fighting Bear, with 250 men, 100 women and 50 children, a total above the 350 given elsewhere. Riley and the NEGenWeb site's other text give 350. For about a month the Pawnee hunted on Beaver and Prairie Dog creeks with great success. Riley calls 1873 the last good year for large-scale hunting in the region.

The Sioux were in the valley in unusual strength. Pawnee Killer's Cut-off Oglala and a Brule band under sub-agent Stephen Estes, who had arrived at the end of July, were camped on the Frenchman and the Stinking Water. According to Riley, the Oglala had a fresh grievance. In early July a party of Ute had raided their horses, and in the pursuit that followed, a Sioux warrior was killed and six wounded. Janis, their sub-agent, had talked the Oglala out of a revenge expedition against the Ute.

On the morning of 3 August, six Oglala warriors reported that they had found a Pawnee party. Janis wrote in a report that the chief Little Wound had asked him whether he had any order to stop him fighting them. Janis said he had none, and that the young men had made up their minds; they reasoned, he wrote, that the Pawnee would treat them as the Ute had if they did not strike first. The Oglala then invited the Brule to join. Estes, in an August report, blamed what followed on Janis's "ignorance and bad advice", and said the Brule had argued that they had as much right to attack as any other band. He said he and his interpreter did everything they could to stop them. Riley adds that the secretary of war, William Belknap, had turned down Estes's request for rations for the Brule on 22 July and authorised sugar and coffee only on 4 August, by which time the Brule were far to the south. He calls it a possibility that the delay irritated them.
The NEGenWeb text says the order of events in the Sioux camps is not easily traced, but that the Cut-off band appears to have been first to find the Pawnee and first to decide to attack.

The Pawnee camped near the present site of Trenton on the night of 4 August. White hide hunters had warned them before that many Sioux were about. Williamson and the Pawnee thought it a trick to scare them out of the buffalo country. That night three more white men came to the camp, and one of them so impressed Williamson with his sincerity that he took him to Sky Chief, who was in command that day.

Williamson recalled the exchange in a later account. Sky Chief called the men liars, said they wanted to drive the Pawnee off so white hunters could take the buffalo for hides, and told Williamson he was a squaw and a coward. Williamson replied: "I will go as far as you dare go. Don't forget that." Riley judges that this was where Williamson failed in his duty: his instructions gave him the authority to compel the Pawnee to follow his judgment, and he let pride overrule it.

On the morning of 5 August the party travelled two miles down the Republican and then turned northwest along the west bank of a canyon that cut through the high divide. Sky Chief apologised to Williamson for his words of the night before, but still sent out no scouts. When buffalo were sighted on the divide, the Pawnee men and their leaders scattered to hunt, leaving the women, children and old men to go on. A young warrior borrowed Williamson's gun, leaving him unarmed.

The Sioux killed several hunters first, and Sky Chief, caught unready, was one of the first to die, in Riley's telling. The women and children were hurried into the canyon while the men regrouped. Williamson and a Pawnee chief agreed that the party should fall back to the trees down the canyon, but Fighting Bear insisted on making a stand where they were, and prevailed. L. B. Platt was a young man from Baltimore who had asked to come on the hunt. Riley has Williamson advise Platt to get away down the canyon, and then ride out with an interpreter under a white flag to parley; the NEGenWeb text has Williamson and Platt riding out together. Both agree the Sioux fired on the party, which fled back to the canyon. In Riley's account Williamson's horse was shot from under him as he reached safety.

According to the NEGenWeb text, in the first hour the Pawnee held their own, since only about a hundred Sioux were present. Then reinforcements arrived. All sources there agree the Sioux then numbered about a thousand, against about 250 Pawnee fighters who also had their families to protect. The canyon was narrow, with low banks. The Sioux took both sides and fired down into the crowd. The Pawnee cut their packs of meat, robes and equipment from the horses and fled down the canyon, and the retreat became a rout.

Williamson wrote years later that the memory he could not shake was of a small Pawnee girl who had fallen from her mother's back, sitting on the ground with her arms raised. He tried to lift her, managed only to touch her hand, and could not go back.

The pursuit ended while most of the fleeing Pawnee were still short of the canyon's mouth. Riley writes that the Sioux then turned back up the canyon to the abandoned goods, and that Pawnee women who had fallen behind were raped and the bodies mutilated, with some burned on piles of camp robes. Why the Sioux broke off after killing relatively few is not known, he says. Williamson believed the arrival of cavalry scared them away, but army reports show that Meinhold's troop was camped about a dozen miles away and heard nothing until survivors arrived. Riley's suggestions are that the Sioux had heard rumours of troops, lost their drive in the excitement, or were drawn to the spoils and prisoners. The NEGenWeb text says that the army papers show the Sioux simply considered the raid over.

Meinhold's company had left Fort McPherson on 30 July for a routine tour of the Republican country. Settlers at Culbertson, two miles west of his camp, heard the shooting from ten miles away. The captain himself first learned of it when Williamson, Fighting Bear and two other chiefs rode in, followed by the first fleeing Pawnee. The chiefs asked for protection and wanted to ride with the army against the Sioux. Meinhold told them to keep going down the valley to the Red Willow settlement and said he would visit the canyon that afternoon.

The cavalry found two survivors, a wounded woman and a badly injured baby, lying in a pool of water. The surgeon, David Powell, made them more comfortable. When the troop returned, the woman was gone and the child had fresh head wounds; Riley says it appeared she had killed it. A trader, William Fitch, found a wounded woman, probably the same one, and carried her by wagon to Indianola, where she died. Powell described the scene in a letter to the Omaha Herald, in which he wrote: "It was a horrible sight."

The army counted 63 dead, 13 men and 50 women and children, according to Riley. The NEGenWeb text instead gives the military count as 57. Burgess's later census at the reservation gave twenty men, thirty-nine women and ten children dead, which is 69, with twelve wounded and several children unaccounted for even after the eleven captives came back. Riley's own summary says approximately 70. Sioux losses are as uncertain. Estes reported one Brule killed and two or three mortally wounded. Janis reported no Oglala dead but two wounded. Weeks later a settler on a hunt came across six fresh Sioux burials in trees near the Stinking Water's mouth, and these have always been assumed to be from the battle.

Riley is critical of the army's follow-up. Meinhold offered to guard a Pawnee party that would come back for the abandoned meat and robes, but the Pawnee did not return, and he marched on. A scouting detachment under Lieutenant Joseph Lawson with the guide Leon Pallardie found only the trail of a war party heading north. Riley finds it hard to believe that Pallardie, who knew the country and the Sioux well, could not find a thousand mounted men, and concludes that he, and perhaps Meinhold, had no wish to. He allows that it may have been foolhardy for fifty-odd soldiers to try.

The Brule handed over their prisoners, two girls, a woman and a boy, to Estes. Janis's Oglala were more reluctant and held seven, three women and four girls aged two to ten. All eleven were returned. The NEGenWeb text credits Estes with the major role in that return, and says Janis, whom it calls the nearest thing to a villain in the story, sent the Pawnee agent a bill for $42.50 for their care, which as far as is known was not paid. Estes took the Brule back to their reservation in Dakota, where they arrived on 27 August.

The Pawnee reached the Red Willow settlement the afternoon of the fight. A young widow working at a store there later recalled that she was told the place was surrounded by Indians. The mourners' chanting and wailing was something the settlers never forgot, Riley says. Williamson bought flour and sugar at the settlement's store for the journey home. The survivors went on to Plum Creek, were treated by a doctor there, and were put on trains.

The agent Burgess sent a reservation teacher, Samuel Longshore, back to the canyon in late August. According to the settler Royal Buck, Longshore recovered about six tons of robes, meat and equipment, much of it from settlers in Red Willow and Hitchcock counties who had already picked over the site. Buck wrote that some of those who had boasted of taking hides claimed afterwards that their goods had been stolen. Williamson was also sent back to bury the dead, most of them placed along the bank and covered with earth pushed down from above.

It was Buck who first called the place Massacre Canyon. After a visit a few days later, he described the canyon floor at its head covered with discarded packs, meat, robes, tents and kettles over fifty yards, and about twenty bodies lying in a pond hole. He found one sign of resistance, a bank where eight warriors had taken shelter and all lay dead with a woman and a child.
content.h2: The end of the Nebraska hunts
content.p: The Pawnee never made another tribal buffalo hunt in Nebraska. In 1875 and 1876 they left for Indian Territory, and their Nebraska lands were sold to the government and opened to settlement. Writers disagree about how much the battle had to do with it. Riley says it has often been claimed that Massacre Canyon was an important factor but that he found no documentation, and that in councils with their agent the battle was hardly mentioned. The NEGenWeb text takes the opposite view: it argues that a majority of Pawnee, particularly the old, had resisted leaving Nebraska, and that after the battle the whole tribe was so demoralised that the faction favouring removal gained support. It also says about fifty Pawnee slipped away that fall to winter with the Wichita, and that the usual winter hunt was cancelled.

The dates of the move are given differently. The Oklahoma Historical Society says the Pawnee gave up their Nebraska reservation in 1874 and moved to Oklahoma over three years, a tribe of about two thousand people settling between the forks of the Arkansas and Cimarron rivers. A 1942 article in the Chronicles of Oklahoma dates the removal to 1874-75 and says that close to one in three Pawnee fell ill and died in the first two years there, cooped up in mudhouses in a wet, malarial region along the Black Bear. Riley and the local history text, quoted above, have them leaving in 1875 and 1876. The Oklahoma encyclopedia records that the tribe's population reached a record low of 629 in 1901.
Williamson stayed with the Pawnee in Indian Territory for several years and then returned to Genoa, where he died on 12 March 1927.

On the fiftieth anniversary in 1923, Trenton's citizens staged the first Massacre Canyon pow-wow, and Sioux survivors came. The event ran annually, except for the war years, into the late 1950s. The 1925 gathering drew survivors from both nations, and the two tribes smoked a pipe of peace together for the first time.

Trenton's editor, A. L. Taylor, conceived the idea of a marker in the early twenties of the century, and a Massacre Canyon Memorial Association was formed. Representative Ashton Shallenberger won $7,500 from Congress for it, which Riley calls one of the few times Congress funded the marking of what can be called a local historical site. Shallenberger had hoped for a statue by Gutzon Borglum, but the money was too little; the shaft was built by R. P. Colling of Indianola. The monument is 35 feet of Minnesota pink granite and weighs 91 tons. About 5,000 people attended its dedication on 26 September 1930. Its inscription, written by the historical society's Addison Sheldon, names Sky Chief, Sun Chief and Fighting Bear as the principal Pawnee chiefs, and Spotted Tail, Little Wound and Two Strikes as the Sioux chiefs. Carved faces on the shaft show John Grass, a Sioux, and a Pawnee chief named Ruling Hisson, whose wife and two children, according to the NEGenWeb text, were killed.

The monument first stood on a hill overlooking the valley. When a new highway was built it was moved to its present site on Highway 34, a few miles east of Trenton. Riley dates the move to the late 1950s; the local history site says the state bought the land in September 1960 and the monument was moved in late 1961. Riley's closing comment is that the state's chief monument to its once most powerful tribe commemorates not their greatness but one of their worst defeats.
